text: Avoid using a single test, grade, or performance as a verdict on ability.
Avoid rescuing at the first sign of frustration when the child can safely attempt the next step.
Avoid praising intelligence in ways that imply being smart is a fixed trait.
Avoid comparing siblings or classmates as a motivational strategy.
Avoid turning every hobby into lessons, rankings, or measurable achievement.
Avoid treating normal mistakes as evidence of laziness or poor character.
Avoid making competition the default structure for every activity.
Avoid solving ordinary peer conflicts before hearing the child's account and helping them think through options.
Avoid using shame to teach responsibility.
Avoid making chores punitive when they are meant to teach contribution.
Avoid filling every unscheduled hour with organized activities.
Avoid using screens as the automatic solution to boredom, frustration, or waiting.
Avoid assuming that screen limits alone teach digital judgment; discuss the reasons behind the rules.
Avoid making food a reward, punishment, or moral scorecard.
Avoid pressuring a child to eat beyond hunger or treating appetite as disobedience.
Avoid treating a child's current academic difficulty as a permanent identity.
Avoid giving vague praise when specific feedback would teach more.
Avoid demanding persistence when the real lesson is that a different strategy is needed.
Avoid expecting adult-level organization from a child who is still learning systems for managing tasks.
Avoid taking over a responsibility immediately after a mistake; use the mistake to teach repair.
Avoid dismissing strong feelings simply because the underlying problem seems small to an adult.
Avoid requiring children to forgive instantly after being hurt.
Avoid assuming every friendship problem is bullying or every conflict is harmless; look at pattern, severity, and context.
Avoid making independence mean the child must solve everything alone.
Avoid treating obedience as the primary evidence of maturity.
